title: Vase (one of a pair)

altText: A tall porcelain vase decorated with birds and butterflies. It is one of a matching pair and stands about half a meter high.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, maker, date, medium, tags (Birds, Butterflies), height, credit line, public-domain flag, and image URLs read from the record

context: A tall porcelain vase made at the Meissen factory near Dresden, Germany, around 1730. The Met catalogs it as one of a pair, and its subject tags are Birds and Butterflies. It is about 49 cm (19 7/16 inches) tall.

descriptions.k: This tall vase is made of shiny porcelain. Birds and butterflies decorate it. It is one of two that match. It is about as tall as a big dog. Can you find a bird? Can you find a butterfly?
descriptions.g12: This vase was made in Germany about three hundred years ago. It is made of hard, shiny porcelain. Birds and butterflies decorate it. It is half a meter tall, and there is a matching vase just like it. Look for the animals. What might they be doing?
descriptions.g35: This tall porcelain vase was made around 1730 at Meissen in Germany, where Europeans first learned to make hard-paste porcelain. It is one of a pair, which means a matching vase once stood with it. The Met says its decoration includes birds and butterflies. Find them. Why might a maker choose animals that fly to decorate something that stands so tall?
descriptions.g68: Around 1730, Meissen was still a young factory proud of making hard-paste porcelain, a material Europeans had once imported from Asia. This vase stands nearly half a meter tall and was made as one of a pair, a common way to decorate a room symmetrically. Birds and butterflies decorate it. How might a pair of tall vases shape the feeling of a room? What can painted animals add to a vessel that may never hold flowers?
descriptions.g910: This Meissen vase of about 1730 belongs to a pair, a format that creates symmetry and display value beyond any practical use. Its large scale and the Met's subject tags, birds and butterflies, show how porcelain painters used animals to animate the surface of a glossy vessel. Consider how pairing, height, and subject matter all signal wealth and refinement, and how a once-secret technique became a basis for prestige and competition among European courts.
descriptions.g1112: Meissen's vases of around 1730 belong to a moment when European porcelain was both a technical achievement and a vehicle for court display. This vase, one of a pair, uses scale and symmetry to claim space in an interior, while its birds and butterflies attach it to a long tradition of decorative nature imagery. The object raises questions about borrowing from Asian porcelain, the role of painters and modelers, and the shifting meanings of a pair when separated into museum collections.

k.shape: What shapes do you see on the vase? Are the wings round, pointy, or both?
k.color: What colors do you see on the animals? Which color is your favorite?
k.texture: Porcelain is smooth and hard. How would this tall vase feel if you touched it gently?
k.space: This vase is as tall as a big dog. Where in a room would you put it?
k.light: Where does the vase look shiniest where the light hits it?
k.meaning: Why do you think the painter chose animals that fly?

teacherNote.context: Meissen, near Dresden, was the first European factory to make hard-paste porcelain. The Met catalogs this vase as one of a pair made around 1730 and tags it Birds and Butterflies.
directions: Have students design a matching pair of vases with a common theme and discuss how symmetry affects the effect.
Ask students to compare the scale of the vase to classroom objects and discuss how scale changes meaning.
Discuss why decorative objects were once made in pairs for display.
